blocks.x: The date is September the 23rd, I believe, 22nd or 23rd, anyway, 1961. There's the calendar over that. And this is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins, interviewing Mr. Robertson. Do you mind giving your full name, Mr. Robertson? Henry Robertson. Henry, any middle name?
You were saying about this, the young Excelsior.

Yeah, the young Excelsior. You see, they had the old Excelsior. Well, so many of the old fellas died out. Well, then lots of them come and say, you know, they'd kill about picking. It'd take like me and several more others who wasn't going to let it go down. We just picked it up and picked up the best men that we knew that could compare with the men that had dropped out. We just renewed the name and went on out again.
Do you have any members in this young Excelsior band that were also in the old Excelsior band?

Me? The fellow played Triney. He played with them. And I think they had three or four was in there. But we were only three. Only three left. The others all practically died out. That's Ewan Wilson and Wilson. And this boy played, Buster played with him several times. But he wasn't, he was young, young, young, young, young, but you couldn't even, you know, count him. Because you couldn't even put him in there. But we got him playing plus nine. But he's just about as good as them as playing the old Excelsior at that time. Yeah, he's good. Yeah, he's very good. Yeah, he's good. We got some fellas from New York down here now. Wants to take us over, some white fellas. But Buster went up there and they took a light on the bus and didn't have any plenty. Him and his sons down here now.
Oh yeah, Crank Bay. Yeah. Crank, something like that.

They want us to get together. And as soon as he can get straight, we going on with him. We ain't gonna take nothing but an old set up. The old style of band. The old set up. Well, if we going on with him, if he falls, we fall too. That's what we figured. If he make it, we make it. And if he don't, well, none of us make it. That's our idea, going along with him. Because he got confidence in us. It's one thing anywhere he put us, we gonna wait. And if it's money there, he'll get it. Because we can wait. If we live, we'll wait. And we're gonna try to put us up on the street, and we're gonna try to help him, and we're gonna help Buster. If he's got good confidence in Buster and he thinks that we can do it, we're gonna try to do it. Because you see all this new type of music now. It's all right for a while. It lasts for a while. But the people coming in now, you take all the northern people, they come here for that type of music. We got bands down there now. Down there, Brooke Carell down there playing on Boybin Street down there now. They have to get away from that new type of music. We don't have to fool ourselves. We got some white bands down there. Gives us plenty hell, white boys. Gives us plenty hell with that Dixieland music. Oh yeah. You see, they can't play. And they're not no old timers. They're young comers. They're part of the gift. Gives us plenty of things. That Dixieland music. That's right. Because the type of music we were playing, the average fellow was playing, they went jump up and left it and went full with this new type of music. And those boys that went on with that, picked up that old time music and went in that old time music, sent them big. And they're on the radio. Yeah, they're on the radio. And they can play it too. Man that's blowing, they can play it. Lots of times I yell on the radio, I said, the time they yell on the radio, I have to shake my head. And one of them is Joe Oliver or Lewis Armstrong. Which one of them is playing? You know, boys right down there. Now you tell, you take this boy, what you call them down there. You got one of the best bands down there in that place. And them colored boys down there, they got to play. You take Sharky, Sharky got a band. And they put bands. They got a good band. We got another fellow down there. They go put it on there playing down there. Sure. You boys and men can play. You see? They have a good band. But now coming out of the brass band, the old time bands here. We don't have no more old time bands. You don't have no more left nines. You have the Herica band. You have the John Kazmi that there, Young Tuxedo. Now you ain't got no more organized band outside Young Excelsior. Now you don't have no organized bands. Old bands. Those bands are only made up bands. Yeah. They make up. They don't have no more study bands like they used to. You see one time you could get out there, you'd hire a band, you'd see that same face today you see tomorrow, you see it the next day. If you hire them for a week, you'd see that same ten faces out there, but you can't do it now. Because they're not organized like they used to. Years ago they're not organized.
What about these dance orchestras? Did you play with any of the earlier dance orchestras, Mr. Robinson?
What the?
Like the dance bands? Who did you play with when years come by? Years ago.
Oh, I used to play with old Buddy P.T.
Oh, you did play with Buddy? Oh yeah, I played all over the lake then. When they had that boat run up in the man. Who did he have in his band then, at that time?

Oh yeah, he had that boat. One of the best clients that we had here, he left here and went to California. His wife died over the river not so long ago. Not good to know, he come from Manneville too, but I didn't know that boy.
What did he play in?
Clining.
Old Clining?
Yeah, yeah. Used to play down in the, in the, in the, the, the, not so long. He stayed there quite a while. He was good, he had a band and he left the other one long. George Lewis?
That's George Lewis.
Oh, George Lewis. George Lewis was playing with us. In Manneville. He used to play with us in Manneville. He said he's still alive. Yeah, he's still alive. Yeah, I know, but he left his wife's.
Yeah, he bought a home over the road and his wife died.

And he came back here and I haven't seen the hood of George Lewis. He still has his home there. He's out on the road now, right now. I ain't seen that man, right there in Manneville. That's why he came. I ain't seen him no more. I ain't seen that man since he needed to be with his wife. Really? I was at the funeral. I ain't seen him in that day to listen. George Lewis, I had a fella at that time we used to call him E-String. We used to call him E. We used to call him Big E. But he was playing with us.
What did he play?
Uh, bass violin.
Oh, bass violin.
Yeah.
How'd he get that name, E-String?
We used to call him E-String because when he first started to learn how to play, he loved to play all the time on the E-String. He was like Eastring. We could call it Eastring.
It wasn't Chester Zardis, wasn't it Chester?
No, no. You talking about Chester Jones?
No, Chester Zardis.
Oh no, it wasn't Chester.
The little fella, he used to jump up and down when he played.

No, it wasn't Chester. I know this other day. Chester. No, it wasn't him. No, this fella here. He belonged in Manderville too. Well, we had a fella. We had a fella out of that in there called Black Eagle. Black Eagle. He was playing trumpet too over there with us. Black Eagle. Yeah. Any time a man played his way out of penitentiary, you know he could play.
Oh yeah.

Yeah, boy, Furan got in trouble over there and used to set up on the wall that damn play trumpet. Used to allow him to blow that trumpet and let him make a little band up in there. Oh yeah. So, them people got him out of there. Yeah. Black Eagle. Little, little, little, little, little, little, little, little, little black black. Probably he could know. You never knew his name or any other name.
That's all I ever know.

We lived in Manderville. Well at the time, my mother was living in Mandeville. I live in here. But we used to go over there and play, you know. Well I'd go still with my mother the whole time. We used to play over there in Covenant, Mandeville, Slidell, because Buddy PT had all that work up and down in the coast. Well he had his bands through there and he'd pick up them fellas through there. He carried me out there with him drummer. And we'd run all through there. That time we used to have, we had an old man playing violin. When I'm trying to think of his name, we were first to play violin. I know y'all wouldn't know him because when I met him, he was quite old and stuff. From across the lake then? Yeah, across the country, he played violin. There was an old time man, that man could play a violin. Old man Mitchell.
Mitchell?
Yeah Old man Mitchell. He was a violin player. And he was good. Well we, Buddy PT and him, we played over there. I played with him.
You never met this clarinet player, Steve Lewis, over there? Did you get to him?
No, I met Steve Lewis here.
Oh you did? Yeah. Oh.
I met Steve Lewis here. I met Steve Lewis. He was a piano player.
Oh, what was it? Steve Lewis. He was a piano player. Oh, what was it? Steve Lewis. You got me off on it.

No, you got, no, you got, yeah, Steve Lewis was a piano. Yeah. Steve was a piano player, yeah. What was it? He used to live right on the second street. He was a second, he was a piano player. I can't think of his name now.
That's who you're talking about. No, it was a clarinetist with the name of Lewis, now I can't think. No?
Now you're hitting your machine now, Steve. Oh, I know what you're talking about. You live in the St. Bernard Project. And she got, yeah, that's the Steve you talking about playing here now?
No, that's Steve Andrews down that way.
Yeah, I know that's Steve down in the St. Bernard Project. He's an old timer. Yeah.
Alfred, he's an old timer.
Yeah, Alfred, he's an old timer.
You know, who else you got there?
I'm going to ask for any other drummers you can remember. Do you remember any Henry Zeno? He was a drummer. Yes, indeed.
I know him Zeno. I know him good.
Who did he play with when you heard him? Do you remember what band he was in?

When I remember knowing him, hearing him playing, really. I think Henry Zeno was playing with the Excelsior. That's who I think he was playing with. Now either when he was playing with the Excelsior or the old tuxedo. It wasn't with the Heirica. Then he was a fella, much like a swing man. Any band would hire him because he was good. He was a great orchestra man. He was a good drummer. Yeah.
Well, do you remember Contrell, man?
Oh, my Contrell? Yeah.
Louis Contrell.

Yeah. You know what I'm talking about? Yeah. Yes, indeed. And Contrell, he's another man. He was Buddy P.T. Know him Buddy P.T. time? He was on there. Louis and Joe Oliver. That's who he was on there with. They had a band down there they called the Creole Serenators. We were down there with them all down in there. That'd be a real, a real Creole band down there. Yeah.
Such a one with Peter Bockeye?

Yeah, well, Peter Bockeye. Hey, there's a P.R.O. neighborhood P.R.O. Yeah, he come over here with Peter Bockeye. This band was Excelsior because he comes over the river. That's why the Excelsior band was stayed there with all them Bockeye, all them Bockeyes from over the river.
You called them Bockeyes? Yeah, I come up with them.
Oh, Bockeyes. Yeah, old man Peter Bockeye, he got a son. All of them, he comes over the river. Yeah, and he still lives over there. Yeah, I live with him.
Yeah, I know. Did you know Manetta? Mania Manetta?
Manetta. Yeah, I know Manetta.
Oh, speaking about the old-time drummers, did you ever know or see Meg Murray or Diddy Channel?
No, I didn't remember. I heard of him. Walter Brundy. Walter Brundy. He was another old-timer. I heard of him. Walter Brundy.
Walter Brundy, he was another old-timer.
I heard him tell about sometimes.
I guess he's way back. Yeah, I think he left here pretty young and he was killed up in Baton Rouge or someplace. Yeah, I heard of those.

50 years ago, 40. Now, they had a fella used to come here out of Donifanville. He used to be here a lot of times. He was a great drummer too, called Bolegs, but he didn't belong here. Bolegs? Yeah, he used to play that band in Donifanville, that great band there in Donifanville, but he didn't belong here. When he came here, them bands were high. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Bolegs, great drummer.
Did he ever play with the Claiborne Williams band? Yeah. That's the best with his drummer. Oh, it was his drummer.
That's the drummer, Claiborne Williams. He married Claiborne Williams' daughter.
You never knew him by any other name? Never knew him by any other name.
He married his daughter. Claiborne Williams' daughter. That's right. Yeah.

That's true. You come off the band. Yeah. That's in the world. Was there any difference much in the old time drummers, the way they played in the street parades, say on the bass drum, did they have any different special beats that they don't use now or do anything different much than they do now? Did they have a cymbal fastened on their drum in those days? Yeah.
I remember, but it wasn't here. Remember when they used to carry the cymbal, it hit this, had a cymbal set there.
Yeah.
They had a cymbal in the hand.
In the hand. Yeah, I've seen that.
Hit on. But later, they changed that. They put the cymbal up there and you take a wire and made it.
Yeah, like your wire beater you had on there.

See, they made a beater like that. Well, that's the difference in that it's just like a sock cymbal. Now that's the difference in that flam, it made too much of noise. Yeah. It made too much of noise and it slapped.
How long ago is it since they did that?

Oh, that's been, I was looking but a boy that did that before I ever started playing music. Changed that. Because I remember when they had, at that time, I was driving, and they had a band. A racer in the band, boy, used to carry the cymbal. The man had a cymbal in his hand and cymbal in the drum. Well, it hit it like that on there. Well, you could hear that thing going across it. Well, it was too much of vibration. So, somehow, I didn't know the idea to change it to that. But the beats in the street now, yeah, we have lots of different beats that the fella adds on in the street that is not wrote in you. So, you got six, eight, four, four times. But a fella can add on, providing if he can still hold his time.
Yeah, put in some extra beats, you know?

Extra beats if he can hold his time. Now, you can fool around there and make the wrong, make extra beats there and get out of time and throw the whole band. Now, you got six, eight, and four, four times, three, four times beats. Well, now, I can take a beat in the street and play just like I'm playing the orchestra. Just like that, continue like that. But when it comes to the break, I know how to hit it. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Now, come back, come back just like that. See? Mm-hmm.
You're hitting four with your right hand and two with your... Yes, yes. See, see, see, you can do the shuffle. Just like that. See?
Come right back there. Be sure you come back on the right time.
Yeah.

That's definitely the beat. If you make one missed beat, you throw the whole band, and you can't get back. You can't get them back. The bass drum can throw the whole band out of time. You can't play. Yeah, they have lots to... They didn't add on a whole lot of different beats. You got some out there beating one beat to measure, two beats to measure. Now, you take the hardest... They're one of the hardest music in the world to play, even if you're playing a funeral. Because it's time, your left foot. It's real slow.
Every time you go up with your...

You come down with your left foot, you come down with that hand. But if you hit off with your right feet, you throw the whole band. You see, everybody's supposed to come down on their left foot. You start off with your left foot? On your left foot, and you hit them. You hit them off that left foot and come down, every man come down on your left foot, you'll be in time. If you're left foot and your right hand... That's right. You'll come down on your left foot. All that music will stay on the level. That's right. Or some of them get started to play any kind of rhythm. That's so much of this new stuff going on now, they want to make the money. Like I said, you just got to know what you're doing. You take like Happy out there, me, lots of the old mafias, a lot of us old drummers, and they got a...oh yeah, old...oh son, few clothes, you know?
Oh yeah, sure, the bass drummer...
Yeah, they take old son, few clothes, and you got this boy here...oh, what's this boy's name right now? I know him good, uptown there, son White. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Son White, he's an old timer.
Yeah.

Son, few clothes, son White, old time drummers. He's been out. He was on back there. Old, old time drummers. Good drummers too. Now we got one now, now...I can't think of him, but he wasn't about no old time, but he got George Williams, well he's not no old time. George Williams started playing music a few years ago. He was young, right? Yeah.
Yeah, George Williams.
He got a band, George Williams Band, but he's not back in that, not back in that bracket.
Well, would you say that you're more or less beating the same now as you, as the old drummers did the same when you were a boy? That's right.
You take a, I'll tell you what band carried it, regular beat, the old timers, the Erika, Sean Casner, and myself. Now those three bands carried it at the same time, tight down, old timers.
Were you going to say something about that funeral, those funeral dirges? You said it was something difficult? Oh yeah. How do you, how do you beat on those?
You see, on a funeral, you got an after beat on a funeral just like this here. Boom.
Boom. Boom, boom.
Then you count, one, two, and you cover on the third beat. Boom.
Boom.

Then your instruments pick up. It's like what you're going to play. Ne-ro-my-go-dee. Ne-ro-my-go-dee. Ne-ro-my-go-dee. Do-dee. Do-dee. Do-dee. Do-dee. Do-dee. Do-dee. That's a different beat. And how are you walking when you're playing on it? Just one, two, just like this here, you're stepping. You see you walking, this is the other guy. I'm sure I can make this here. Yeah, don't just stay on the stage. It's just like that, you see that left foot? You start on the left. Mm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm have a funeral, they got the certain men that they can use to play. You take snare drummer, like this man here, you take him, the snare drummer, you can't take the average man who can play a funeral equal with him, because he knows the role between the times and the beats and the layout, and that's what that snare drummer got to know. For this bass drummer to come in, this bass drummer follow him, every time he said blump, blump, blump, boom, and then he loads. And he gets it in there and he goes, boom, and he says, blump, blump, blump, boom. That's just the way he goes. Go around the other door there. Go around the other door. So that's the way the funeral to do goes on. It's different all together from any other type of music. That's actually called, when you're playing that, you better have your head if you ain't got that music in front. If you ain't got that in front while you're looking at it, you better sure have it in your head. You can't mess up with them. That's why they got to pick different men out of different bands to play. Every time they have a fune, you practically see me out there, because they come and hustle me up. You make your head look away, I say, yeah, come on, blump.
You enjoy that? You enjoy that? You know the whole jazz you said?

Oh yeah. It's been enjoying when you're out there with those fellas who knows how to play. I mean, you could be the bunch of knows how to play. It's enjoying. You know the people. They're satisfied. See them dancing and kicking up and it's joyful. What you want?
It's alright.
It's going on. What's going on? Well, it's my mind playing.

I was going to ask about the bass drum. You know the bass drum doesn't play all the time on the street. The snare drum in between the pieces. Yes, snare drum kick has all the time. Was there ever a time when the bass drum would play with the snare drum?

No. Sometimes those fellas just do it, you know, say ordinary parades like that. The bass drum go along like that. But you don't have to. But that snare drum can't time all the time until it's time to play. Then the bass drum come in. But the bass drum, the fact of it, he don't work as hard as the snare drum. The snare drum don't never have no rhythm. He always works. The bass drum. If they walk two blocks, he can walk two blocks in the north. If they walk two blocks in the north. If they walk two blocks in the north. If they walk two blocks in the north. If they walk two blocks in the north. But that snare drum has got to still keep that time from the walk by.
Of course you have the job carrying that big bass drum. Yours isn't awfully big as how big is it. No, they all make them small now. Is that 22 inches or something?

Yeah, that's the 22. Now you see the children here, it's just a bigger drummer than that. See, they're getting away from that type of drummer. That drum was too big. It was too big. It was killing drummers.
Can you come around there, please?

She would have a… she wanted to see what it's all about. She used to try to… one time she was taking up music. She was there. We were writing a song. She was writing some songs. A fellow out there. Oh, you know how these young people there. She had several out of New York. She sung several pieces up there. She sung a contract back there for the… she went out there. It made me angry and I wouldn't prove it. Go ahead.
Did you ever play snare drum, Thomas, or other songs? Yeah. Oh, you did play snare drum?

I liked it that better than I did bass drum. Oh, you did, huh? Yeah, but they don't let me play no snare drum. Every time they want me on bass drum, they don't want somebody else on snare drum. And I'd rather play snare drum than play bass drum. I'd get the kick out of playing snare drum, but they'd rather me play bass drum.
Did you have any special beat of your own? Yeah. I know someone do have. Yeah, man.

What kind of a beat did you have? I had a… I got a beat out of the one, man. I'd take my snare drum, man. I'd put all the beats to them one. Bluff, bluff, bluff… Yeah, man. Yeah, to have fun with them. It's like a little bridge in there. And I can take it down there and show you.
I know nobody now. I thought you didn't give an idea of it by humming it over.
Yeah, I give you an idea how I actually do it.
What kind of snare drum do you have? Is it a little thin one or fairly deep? No, I have one. It's not too deep. Regular old time. Wood or metal? Wood.
Vestone and drums. The other drum. Same type of wood I can.
What is that a leader you say?
That's right. Same type. Same type.
Is this little word out here a king? Is that on there?
That's where the little painted on it. Put that sign on there. He's a good printer. He is. Nice printer.
When you played the dance band, how many traps do you have? Do you have the cymbals and what else?
Oh yeah.
Cowbells or wood blocks? Yeah.
What do you use? Yeah, all that in there. The whole... I got a tum tum nothing big. Big tum. Oh yeah, I got a tum tum big as that thing.
Yeah, the recorder.
The stand is pretty hot. This is. That's what stands for it over there.
Oh yes, I see. Yeah, where they find the stands.

It stands for the tum tum and it stands for the sock tum. You see, what makes me keep them like that, when I don't use them, I sit on and sign them and put them in. And fix that. See, I fix them like that. See, I always like that. Fix them nice. So I keep them, so when I have to have them, use them, you know. Everything is alright. That's what I do. I drum. I take my drums and wipe them and everything. Keeps them brushed up.
So once I have to go out with them. It's nice to have them already.
Yeah, they always... Some fellas put the instruments down and never take them until they get ready to play. I don't know. I keep smiling.
Do you ever alter the tension on the heads? Well. Do you tighten them up or loosen them?

See, you loosen them, yeah. Because now you see, when it's hot, you can hear if they say bump. Now what you got to do is you got to slack them all the way around. Now when it gets real cold, you're going to hear us tightening ourselves. So you tighten yourself up. Then you go there and touch it. You see just about how tight and then you slack off. You know? So I go off all the way around. I can give up. So she can always keep her so she can give and tighten up. She can tighten up.

Well I was going to ask, well I think of it, if you have any old photographs of, oh, 30 or 40 years ago or longer back. So many real old bands, you know, the old time, like the old Excelsior band or anything of that kind. No, I don't have any other. You remember a boy. Now most people didn't bother to save the pictures.

I just wondered if you had it right there. No, we didn't have none of them way back. I had some when I was over the river, whatever, I guess, by moving around, you know, tripping around a little. Just like these, yeah, this B-Law, this is what I had to say. The B-Law's about, the best one I had is up in that thing there. Didn't have this or that, but I don't know. Yeah, I had it in a, why I had it so long, because I had it in a, in a bag, and a couple of years ago I put it up there in that frame. So I keep one of them, but I don't usually do with them, you know.
We have a lot of later pictures of parades and all, just hoping to find some of those real old bands. I was going to ask about Manuel Perez and the Onward band. Oh yeah, old, yeah.

I, oh yeah, I play with old, Perez, Onward band. Years ago I went along with them, you know, play extra with them, you know. I play with all them old band actually. They come and get me. Mad drums sometimes, sometimes bassmen, all them old times. All those old time bands, they, they went out so, certainly, when this new stuff come in, old bands, look like they just went out. I tell you what started that, those school bands. See the people tried to pull me those school bands, you know. Yep. And Perez rather than the higher bands pay the money to get the school bands for less than nothing. Bands just went down. Men got scattered. Now I mean you could get them together. Now the people is calling for that type of back, and it's hard to get the men back. You take a lot of them and give it up. Not playing anymore. Not everything you can get out. They got the instruments, they got the instruments there man. Been laying up, they got instruments in there. When they opened the case, they looked at it. Look like it's been there a hundred years. Yeah, haven't touched it for you. Oh, I don't fool that no more. Ain't nothing in it no more. I don't even give it up. I couldn't get nothing out of it. People want something for nothing. I have seen myself playing music, honest and true, for a dollar a night. At them times they didn't call them cavalry, they called them tunks, hunky-tunk. Well I see myself, we had five or six men playing in the band, getting a dollar, a dollar, a dollar, a dollar a night, a piece. I believe you're right here in this city.
I've heard about that too. I played it, I played it.
I played it.

segments.chapter: Young Excelsior and the old-time band scene
segments.title: Interview opening; reviving the Young Excelsior band
segments.summary: Russell and Collins open the session. Robertson explains that he and others renewed the Excelsior name after the old members died out, with only three originals left.

segments.chapter: Young Excelsior and the old-time band scene
segments.title: Old-style bands versus new music; white Dixieland bands; lost organized bands
segments.summary: Robertson says he and the band will back a leader sticking to the old style, comments on white Dixieland bands on Bourbon Street, and laments that bands are no longer organized or steady.

segments.title: Playing with Buddy Petit around the lake; George Lewis in Mandeville
segments.summary: Asked about early dance bands, Robertson says he played with Buddy Petit, who had a boat run on the lake, and recalls George Lewis playing with them in Mandeville.

segments.title: The bass player nicknamed E-String; Chester Zardis ruled out
segments.summary: Robertson explains that the bass violinist E-String got his name from always playing on the E string; Russell asks if it was Chester Zardis, and Robertson says no.

segments.title: Black Eagle the trumpeter and Buddy Petit's work across the lake
segments.summary: Robertson talks about Black Eagle, a trumpeter who played his way out of prison, then about living in Mandeville and playing with Buddy Petit's bands up the coast with old man Mitchell on violin.

segments.title: Confusion over which Steve Lewis the interviewers mean
segments.summary: Collins and Russell try to pin down a Steve Lewis, a pianist or clarinetist, and settle on a Steve in the St. Bernard Project.

segments.title: Drummer Henry Zeno and the bands he played with
segments.summary: Robertson remembers hearing Henry Zeno, who played with Excelsior or Tuxedo and was good enough that any band would hire him.

segments.title: Louis Cottrell, the Creole Serenaders and Peter Bocage
segments.summary: Robertson recalls Cottrell playing in Buddy Petit's time and a Creole band with Oliver, then Peter Bocage and the Excelsior band's ties to musicians from across the river.

segments.title: Other old-time drummers: Manetta, Brundy, Bolegs and Claiborne Williams
segments.summary: Asked about old drummers, Robertson says he knew Manetta, only heard of Walter Brundy, and describes Bolegs from Donaldsonville, who married Claiborne Williams' daughter.

segments.title: How cymbals were mounted on the bass drum over time
segments.summary: Robertson describes the old practice of carrying a cymbal in the hand, later replaced by a mounted cymbal with a beater, because the old way made too much noise.

segments.title: Street beats, adding extra beats and keeping time with the left foot
segments.summary: Robertson demonstrates how bass drummers can add beats in the street if they hold time, and explains that everyone steps off on the left foot to keep the band together.

segments.title: Old-time drummers Son Fewclothes and Son White; bands that kept the regular beat
segments.summary: Robertson names old-time drummers like Son Fewclothes and Son White, mentions George Williams as a newer drummer, and says three old bands carried the regular beat.

segments.title: Beating funeral dirges and why funerals need chosen drummers
segments.summary: Robertson demonstrates the funeral beat, explains the snare drummer leading and the bass drum following, and says he is often hired for funerals.

segments.title: Bass drum versus snare drum in parades; shrinking drum sizes
segments.summary: Robertson explains the bass drum comes in only when the snare cues it, that the snare works harder, and that the 22-inch bass drum replaced bigger, punishing ones.

segments.title: Preferring snare drum; his own beat and snare drum
segments.summary: Robertson says he would rather play snare drum but is always asked for bass drum, describes his own snare beat and his wooden snare drum.

segments.title: Dance band drum kit and how he looks after and tunes his drums
segments.summary: Robertson describes his traps, stands and cymbals, how he keeps his drums wiped and ready, and loosens or tightens the heads with the weather.

segments.title: Searching for old photographs of the early bands
segments.summary: Russell asks about old photographs; Robertson has none from way back and kept only a framed one.

segments.title: Playing with Manuel Perez and the Onward band; decline of old bands and low pay
segments.summary: Robertson played extra with Perez and the old bands, says school bands and the new music killed them off, and recalls working for a dollar a night.
